title: Pàdraig mac Ruairidh's death
summary: The clerk who wrote Leabhar nam Bràithrean in King Iain Ciar's praise dies some years before his king, and no scribe comes after him to keep the tale of the grain law's slow lapsing as he had kept the tale of the war itself.

title: The reeve's price complaint at An Taigh-seinnse Òir
summary: A custodians' reeve who has eaten the house's secret syrupped beef twice a winter for a decade writes into the charter-roll that the price has risen three years running with nothing else about the dish improved, and asks for a second helping in the same breath.

title: The keeper's itemised bill
summary: When the snow that trapped a party of reeves at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta finally lifts, the house's keeper sends after them, by the first cart through, a bill for every jar of pickled spinach and every cup of fire milk they took, itemised, and it is paid in full.

title: Seumas mac Iain gives up the deep keel
summary: After a year of Manannan's priests preaching against his sunken hull, the boat-builder of Seann Skell builds no more deep keels, and keeps his harbour shed mending ordinary boats for ordinary fares until his death.

title: The shrine carried whole to Caol bheag
summary: The fishers who leave Caol ìseal's silted harbour carry their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, and set the shrine up again at Caol bheag stone by stone in the same order, so that it stands as it always stood.

title: Iseabail nic Lachlainn sent out on the king's road
summary: The steward of the royal household at Cathair dhearg, wanting a linen-maid's quick-eared daughter out from under his feet, sends her out with a mule and a letter of lodging to gather what the shires' kitchens and rope-walks still sing at their work.

title: A rope-maker's guess at the old words
summary: A young man of Tormod Ròpaire's crew, not yet trusted with the lead, tells the gatherer Iseabail that Òran na Druime's strange words are likely only older speech worn smooth by centuries of mouths that never meant to wear it; Tormod answers that it changes nothing about how the strand is walked.

title: Òran na Druime read at the king's court
summary: Iseabail nic Lachlainn reads her whole gathering before the king's hall at Cathair dhearg, and Òran na Druime's strange lines silence a room grown used to songs it half knows already; an old harper and a vein-house clerk each say the words fit no tongue or hand they know, and neither can say more than that.

title: Death of Tormod Ròpaire
summary: The rope-maker who led the walk that sang Òran na Druime dies at Cuan shean, seventy years old, having in his last years let a younger man keep the count while he sang on behind him; his crew keeps the song after him exactly as he gave it, no better understood than before.

title: Seann Tarr becomes a village again
summary: With its harbour broken past mending and its boats gone to Cuan ruadh, Seann Tarr keeps its houses and its shrine but is entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village once more rather than a harbour town.

title: The older southern harbours follow the new lane
summary: A season or two after Caol fhiadhaich's boats are first believed, the older harbours of the south coast, which had never in memory put a boat past their own headlands, begin one after another to follow Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich down to the landing at Cidhe Beag.

title: Iseabail's tablets entered in Taigh na Fèithe
summary: On Iseabail nic Lachlainn's death the household she served the rest of her life sends her whole collection to Taigh na Fèithe, where the clerks write into the inventory that it holds one item they can describe only by its sound and its keeping, not its meaning.

title: Caol ìseal turns to the plough
summary: The houses of Caol ìseal nearest the silted water turn to farming the ground behind them after the fishers go east, and within two generations the town that smelled of fish and tar smells, most days, of turned earth.

title: Birth of Catrìona Bheag
summary: A daughter, Catrìona, is born into Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house; she is small from the cradle, and the house calls her Catrìona Bheag.
